speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon, everyone.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Welcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand the hardship that high inflation is causing, and we remain strongly committed to bringing inflation back down to our 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Price stability is the responsibility of the Federal Reserve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Without price stability, the economy does not work for anyone.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In particular, without price stability, we will not achieve a sustained period of strong labor market conditions that benefit all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Since early last year, the FOMC has significantly tightened the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have raised our policy interest rate by 5¼ percentage points and have continued to reduce our securities holdings at a brisk pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The stance of policy is restrictive—meaning that tight policy is putting downward pressure on economic activity and inflation—and the full effects of our tightening have yet to be felt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Today, we decided to leave our policy interest rate unchanged and to continue to reduce our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Given how far we have come, along with the uncertainties and risks we face, the Committee is proceeding carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will make decisions about the extent of additional policy firming and how long policy will remain restrictive based on the totality of the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Recent indicators suggest that economic activity has been expanding at a strong pace and well above earlier expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the third quarter, real GDP is estimated to have risen at an outsized annual rate of 4.9 percent, boosted by a surge in consumer spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: After picking up somewhat over the summer, activity in the housing sector has flattened out and remains well below levels of a year ago, largely reflecting higher mortgage rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Higher interest rates also appear to be weighing on business fixed investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market remains tight, but supply and demand conditions continue to come into better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Over the past three months, payroll job gains averaged 266,000 jobs per month, a strong pace that is nevertheless below that seen earlier in the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate remains low at 3.8 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Strong job creation has been accompanied by an increase in the supply of workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor force participation rate has moved up since late last year, particularly for individuals aged 25 to 54 years, and immigration has rebounded to pre-pandemic levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nominal wage growth has shown some signs of easing, and job vacancies have declined so far this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Although the jobs-to-workers gap has narrowed, labor demand still exceeds the supply of available workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation remains well above our longer-run goal of 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Total PCE prices rose 3.4 percent over the 12 months ending in September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 3.7 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has moderated since the middle of last year, and readings over the summer were quite favorable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But a few months of good data are only the beginning of what it will take to build confidence that inflation is moving down sustainably toward our goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The process of getting inflation sustainably down to 2 percent has a long way to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Despite elevated inflation, longer-term inflation expectations appear to remain well anchored, as reflected in a broad range of surveys of households, businesses, and forecastters, as well as measures from financial markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed’s monetary policy actions are guided by our mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I are acutely aware that high inflation imposes significant hardship as it erodes purchasing power, especially for those least able to meet the higher costs of essentials like food, housing, and transportation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are highly attentive to the risks that high inflation poses to both sides of our mandate, and we are strongly committed to returning inflation to our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I noted earlier, since early last year, we have raised our policy rate by 5¼ percentage points, and we have decreased our securities holdings by more than $1 trillion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our restrictive stance of monetary policy is putting downward pressure on economic activity and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Committee decided at today’s meeting to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 5¼ to 5½ percent and to continue the process of significantly reducing our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are committed to achieving a stance of monetary policy that is sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation sustainably down to 2 percent over time, and to keeping policy restrictive until we are confident that inflation is on a path to that objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are attentive to recent data showing the resilience of economic growth and demand for labor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Evidence of growth persistently above potential, or that tightness in the labor market is no longer easing, could put further progress on inflation at risk and could warrant further tightening of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Financial conditions have tightened significantly in recent months, driven by higher longer-term bond yields, among other factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Because persistent changes in financial conditions can have implications for the path of monetary policy, we monitor financial developments closely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In light of the uncertainties and risks, and how far we have come, the Committee is proceeding carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will continue to make our decisions meeting by meeting, based on the totality of the incoming data and their implications for the outlook for economic activity and inflation as well as the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In determining the extent of additional policy firming that may be appropriate to return inflation to 2 percent over time, the Committee will take into account the cumulative tightening of monetary policy, the lags with which monetary policy affects economic activity and inflation, and economic and financial developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to bringing inflation back down to our 2 percent goal and to keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Reducing inflation is likely to require a period of below-potential growth and some softening of labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Restoring price stability is essential to set the stage for achieving maximum employment and stable prices over the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: To conclude: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We at the Fed will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you, and I look forward to your questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thanks for your question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, I’ll talk about bond yields, but I want to take a second and just sort of set the broader context in which we’re looking at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, if you—if you look at the situation—let’s look at the economy first.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has been coming down, but it’s still running well above our 2 percent target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market has been rebalancing, but it’s still very tight by many measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: GDP growth has been strong, although many forecasters are forecasting, and they have been forecasting, that it will slow.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As for the Committee, we are committed to achieving a stance of monetary policy that’s sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation down to 2 percent over time, and we’re not confident yet that we have achieved such a stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that is the broader context into which this, this strong economy and all the things I said—that’s the context in which we’re looking at this question of rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, obviously we’re monitoring, we’re attentive to the increase in longer-term yields and—which have contributed to a tightening of broader financial conditions since the summer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I mentioned, persistent changes in broader financial conditions can have implications for the path of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In this case, the tighter financial conditions we’re seeing—[coming] from higher long-term rates, but also from other sources, like the stronger dollar and lower equity prices—could matter for future rate decisions, as long as two conditions are satisfied.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The first is that the tighter conditions would need to be persistent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that is something that remains to be seen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s critical.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Things are fluctuating back and forth—that’s not what we’re looking for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: With financial conditions, we’re looking for persistent changes that are material.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The second thing is that, that the longer-term rates that have moved up—they can’t simply be a reflection of, of expected policy moves from us that we would then—that if we didn’t follow through on them, then the rates would come back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, and I would say on that, it does not appear that an expectation of higher near-term policy rates is causing the increase in longer-term rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, in the meantime, though, perhaps the most important thing is that these higher Treasury yields are showing through to higher borrowing costs for households and businesses and those higher costs are going to weigh on economic activity to the extent this tightening persists and the mind’s eye goes to the 8 percent—near 8 percent mortgage rate, which could have pretty significant effect on housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s how I would answer your question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s exactly right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, to say it a different way: We haven’t made any decisions about, about future meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have not made a determination, and we’re not—I will say that we’re not confident at this time that we’ve reached such a stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not confident that we haven’t; we’re not confident that we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s—that is—the way we’re going to be going into these future meetings is to be, you know, just determining the extent of any additional further policy tightening that may be appropriate to return inflation to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, let me start by saying we haven’t made a decision about September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re asking a hypothetical there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’re going into December meeting—we’ll get, as you know, two more inflation ratings, two more labor market readings, some data on, on economic activity, and so we’ll be taking—and also the broader situation, the broader financial condition situation and broader world situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll be looking at all those things as we make a decision in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We haven’t made that decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would say, though, that, that the idea that if you—the idea that would—difficult to raise again after stopping for a meeting or two, it’s just not right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, the Committee will always do what it thinks is appropriate at the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, again, we haven’t made any decisions about—at all about December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We didn’t even—we didn’t talk about making a decision in December today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Really, it was a decision for this meeting and understanding broader things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I guess I don’t want to answer your question about the—about the recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the answer is “no.” I think I have to answer it, since we did publicly say in the minutes—you’ll know anyway in the [next] minutes—the staff did not put a recession back in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, it would be hard to see how you would do that if you look at the—look at the activity we’ve seen recently, which is not really indicative of a recession in the near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of how to think about translation into rate hikes, I think it’s just too early to be doing that, and the main reason is we just don’t know how persistent this will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can see how volatile it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Different kinds of news will affect the level of rates, and I think any kind of an estimate that was precise would hang out there and have a great chance of looking wrong very quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think what we can say is that financial conditions have clearly tightened, and you can see that in the rates that, that consumers and households and businesses are paying now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And over time, that will have an effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We just don’t know how persistent it’s going to be, and it’s tough to try to translate that in a way that I’d be comfortable communicating into how many rate hikes that is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, I just—that’s, you know, the way our policy works is—and sometimes it works with lags, of course, which can be long and variable, but ultimately, if you raise interest rates, you do see those effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you see those effects in the economy now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You see what’s happening in the housing market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re seeing that now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’ll see, if you look at surveys of people, it’s not a good time they think to buy durable goods of various kinds because rates are so high now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mention again, we’re getting reports from housing that the effects of this—of this could be quite significant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This has been a resilient economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s, I think, been surprising in its resilience.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And there are a number of possible reasons why that may be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our job is to—is to achieve maximum employment and price stability, and so we take the economy as it comes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It has been resilient, so we just—we take it as it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ve identified those factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those were not meant to be the only factors or a specific test that we’re going to be applying with some metrics behind it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Really, we’re going to be looking at the broader picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll be looking at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, growth—we look at growth insofar as it has implications for our two mandate goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We look at that, and we look at broader financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ll be looking at all of those things as we reach a judgment, you know, whether we need to further tighten policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, if we do reach that judgment, then we will further tighten policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s, it’s—the fact is the Committee is not thinking about rate cuts right now at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not talking about rate cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That is the question we’re focusing on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And what we’ve said there is that we’ll keep policy restrictive until we’re confident that inflation is on a sustainable path down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’ll be the next question, but honestly, right now we’re really tightly focused on the first question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The question of rate cuts just doesn’t come up because I think the first—it’s so important to get that first question, you know, as close to right as you can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not—it’s not, you know—that is the question, and you’re right that, in September, we wrote down one additional rate hike.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know—and we’ll [each] write down another forecast, as you know, in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, there are significant issues out there, as you point out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Global geopolitical tensions are certainly elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that goes for the war in Ukraine; it goes for the war between Israel and Hamas.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re monitoring that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our job is to monitor those things for their economic implications.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, the UAW strike, as you point out is—appears to be coming to an end.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Oil prices have flattened out; they haven’t gone down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I guess they’ve gone down a little bit from their earlier peak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Another one is the possibility of government shutdown; we don’t know about that one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there’s plenty of risk out there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I would go back to—the bigger picture from our standpoint is, we’ve got a very strong economy, strong labor market, making progress on the labor market, making progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re very focused on getting confident that we have achieved a stance of monetary policy that is sufficiently restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s really our focus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t say I was terribly surprised.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I was very impressed by York as a town with a real strategy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I would say it’s very impressive what the people there have put together in the face of, you know, some difficult longer-run trends about offshoring of manufacturing and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’ve done a great job as a city, I think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, what you hear—and it’s consistent there—which is people are really suffering under high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You were there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We talked to some people who, you know, were feeling that in their businesses and other people who were feeling it in their home lives as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s painful for people—particularly people who don’t have a lot of extra financial resources who are spending most of their incoming, you know, income on the essentials of life.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That wasn’t new.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that did come through very clearly in, in the conversations we had in York, and, you know, I walked away from that even—you know, I mean, just thinking that we really—the best thing we can do for the U.S. is to restore price stability—fully restore price stability and not fail in that task and do it as quickly as possible, but also with the least damage we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, I think everyone has been very gratified to see that we’ve been able to achieve, you know, pretty significant progress on inflation without seeing the kind of increase in unemployment that has been very typical of rate hiking cycles like this one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s, that’s a historically unusual and very welcome result.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the same is true of growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’ve been saying that we need to see below-potential growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And growth has been strong, but yet we’re still seeing this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think I still believe, and my colleagues for the most part I think still believe, that is likely to be true.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is still likely to be true—not a certainty—but likely that we will need to see some slower growth and some softening in the labor market—in labor market conditions to get, you know, to fully restore price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—but it’s only a good thing that we haven’t seen it, and I think we know why.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, since, since we lifted off, we, we have understood that there are really two processes at work here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: One of them—one of which is the unwinding of the distortions to both supply and demand [that arose] from the pandemic and the response to the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the other is, is, you know, restrictive monetary policy, which is moderating demand and giving the supply side time to recover—time and space to recover.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you see those two forces now working together to bring down inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s that first one can bring down inflation without the need for higher unemployment or slower growth, it’s just—it’s supply—you know, supply-side improvements like shortages and bottlenecks and that kind of thing going away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s getting, you know, a significant increase in the size of the labor market now, both from labor force participation and from immigration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s a big supply-side, you know, gain that is really helping the economy, and it’s part of why—part of why GDP is so high is because we’re getting that supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, we welcome that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I think those things will run their course, and we’re probably still going to be left—we think, and I think—we’ll still be left with some ground to cover to get back to full price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s where monetary policy and what we do with demand is still going to be important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I continue to think it’s very hard to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s been one year at this meeting—one year ago, this was the fourth of our 75 basis points hikes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s a full year since then.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we are seeing the effects of, of all the hiking we did last year and this year—we’re seeing it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s very hard to know exactly what that might be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you can, for example—an example where you wouldn’t have felt this yet is, is debt that had been termed out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s going to come due and have to get rolled over next year or the year after.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—and there are little things like that where the effects have just taken time to get into the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I don’t—I think we have to make monetary policy under great uncertainty about how long the lags are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think trying to make a clear—get a clear answer and say, “I’m just going to assume this is really not a good way to do it.” And this is one of the reasons why we have slowed the process down this year, was to give monetary policy time to get into the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it takes time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know that, and you can’t rush it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, doing—slowing down is giving us, I think, a better sense of, of how much more we need to do, if we need to do more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well so, let’s talk about the dot plot first.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the dot plot is a picture in time of what the people in the Committee think is likely to be appropriate monetary policy in light of their own personal economic forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In principle, when things change, it’s not—that’s not, like, planned that anybody’s agreed to or that we will do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s a forecast that would change, for example—I mean, many things could change that would cause people to say, “I wouldn’t write down that dot six weeks later.” Think of the number of things that could change your mind on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think the efficacy of the dot plot probably decays over the three-month period between that meeting and the next meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, nonetheless, it’s out there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t—we do personally update our forecast, but we don’t formally update the dot plot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, I think we try to be as transparent as we can about the way we’re thinking about these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re laying out there our thinking, and, you know, as we approach the meeting, we’ll all be—my colleagues and I will be talking about how we’re processing that data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of—so we’re not really changing the way—in terms of growth, what I said was “below potential.” So what you have here recently is growth that is—that is temporarily—potential growth is elevated for a year or two right now over its trend level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: People think trend growth over a long period of time is a little bit less than 2 percent, or I would say just around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But what we’ve had is, with the—with the, you know, improvement in the size of the labor force, as I mentioned, through both participation and immigration, and with the, the, you know, the better functioning in the labor market and with the—with the, you know, the unwinding of the supply chain and shortages and those kinds of things, you’re seeing actually elevated potential growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s catch-up growth that can happen in potential.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that means that if you’re growing—you could be growing at 2 percent this year and still be growing below the increase in the potential output of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I hope that’s clear.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s really what’s going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s why I would say it as below potential.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, I don’t know that I want to just accept anybody’s characterization, but I’ll tell you how we’re doing this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, we’re going meeting by meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re asking ourselves whether we’ve achieved a stance of policy that is sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation down to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s the question we’re asking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re looking at the full range of economic data, including financial conditions and all of those things that we look at, and then we’re, we’re—you know, we’ve, we’ve come very far with this rate hiking cycle, very far.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you saw the spread at the September meeting of—you know, it’s a relatively small spread of—people think one or two additional hikes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’re close to the—to the end of the cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s—that was an impression as of, I believe, as of September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not a promise or a plan of the future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we’re going into these meetings one by one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re looking at the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I mentioned, we’re also—we’re being careful.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re proceeding carefully because we can proceed carefully at this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Monetary policy is restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We see its effects, particularly in interest-sensitive spending and other channels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s how I think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the Committee is not considering changing the pace of balance sheet runoff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not something we’re talking about or considering, and I know there are many candidate explanations for why rates have been going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And QT is certainly on that list.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It may be playing a relatively small effect, although I would say at $3.3 trillion in reserves, it’s not—I think—I think it’s hard to make a case that reserves are even close to scarce at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s not something that we’re—that we’re looking at right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, that proposal is out for comment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we expect a lot of comment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We won’t get those comments until the end of, well, into next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’ve extended the deadline.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ll take them seriously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll read them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll say what, what I do expect is that we will—we will come to a—we’re a consensus-driven organization.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll come to a package that has broad support on the Board.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It means broad support.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We look at a very wide range of financial conditions and, in fact, as you’ll know, different organizations publish different financial conditions’ indexes, which can have, you know, 7 or 8 variables, or they can have 100 variables, so there’s a very rich environment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we tend to look at a few of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not going to give you the names, but, you know, they’re a few of the common ones that people look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so they’re looking at things like the level of the dollar, the level of equity prices, the level of rates, the credit spreads.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sometimes they’re pulling in credit availability and things like that, so it isn’t any one thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We would never look at, for example, long-term Treasury rates in isolation, nor would we ignore them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we would look at them as part of a broader picture, and they do play a role, of course, in many of the major standard financial condition indexes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Banking stress—so it’s something we’re watching.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As you know, we, we did have—there were issues with interest rate risk and also funding uninsured deposits in the March—the things we went through in March and thereafter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we’ve been working a lot with financial institutions to make sure that they have good funding plans and good—and that they have a plan for how to deal with the kind of portfolio, unrealized, losses that they have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we do think the banking system is quite resilient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We had, you know, a handful of bank failures but—so that’s, that’s what we’re out there doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we don’t have any reason to think that this—that these rate hikes are materially changing that picture, which is one of a strong banking system and one where there’s a strong focus by banks and by supervisors on liquidity, on funding, and those sorts of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, so you’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We put a proposal out for comment, is what we did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, this is a job that Congress assigned us, as you, of course, know, in Dodd-Frank, and all we can really do is faithfully implement the statute.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s all we’re trying to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a 90-day comment period, and we typically don’t comment on these things once they’re out for—out for comment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we do hope that stakeholders—and we know that they will use this opportunity to express their views.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They haven’t been shy about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s, that’s critical and that’s, that’s what I can say about that now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, the, the progress is probably going to come in lumps and be bumpy, but we’re making progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I think the core PCE [inflation rate] came down by almost 60 basis points in the third quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the best thing I could point you to would be the September SEP where, you know, the expectation was that, that inflation by the end of next year, on a 12-month trailing basis, would be well into the 2s and the year after that, further into the 2s.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s, that’s—if you look historically, that’s, that’s sort of consistent with the way inflation comes down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It does take some time, and as you get—you know, as you get further and further from those highs, it may actually take longer time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the good news is, you know, we’re making progress and monetary policy is restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we feel like we’re on a path to make more progress, and it’s essential that we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s always the question we’re asking ourselves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we know that, if we fail to restore price stability, the risk is that expectations of higher inflation get entrenched in the economy, and we know that that’s really bad for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation will be both more—both higher and more volatile.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s a—that’s a prescription for misery, and, and so we’re really committed to not letting that happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, for the first year or so of our tightening cycle, the risk was all on the side of not doing enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re, you know, we’re—we’ve come far enough that, that the risks, you know, have gotten more two sided.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can’t identify that with a lot of precision, but it does feel like the, the risks are more two sided now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And—but we’re committed to getting inflation back down to our target over time, and we will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We haven’t really—we haven’t really been thinking about that yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We—you know, it’s November 1, and that’s a decision we’ll be making in the first quarter of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We look at a range of, of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think the, the, the, you know, the UM thing got blown out of proportion a little bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It was actually a preliminary estimate that got revised away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I said it was preliminary in it, but that didn’t get picked up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we look at many, many things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So really, look across the broad array of surveys and also market-based estimates, and, you know, we do that really carefully at every meeting and between meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, there’s—it’s just clear that inflation expectations are in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The public does believe that inflation will get back down to 2 percent over time,.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it will—they’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—and there’s no real crack in that—in that armor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can always find one reading that is a little bit out of whack, but, honestly, the bulk of them are just very clear that the public believes that inflation will come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s, of course—we believe that’s critical in winning the battle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So first thing to say is that it’s very important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a very important variable in, in the way we think about monetary policy, but you can’t identify it with any precision in real time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you have to just take that—you have to take your estimate of it with a grain of salt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What we know now is, you know, within a range of estimates of the neutral rate policy, is restrictive, and it’s therefore putting downward pressure on economic activity, hiring, and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we do—we do talk about this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s not any debate or attempt to, you know, to sort of agree as a group on what—whether r* has moved or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Some people think it has, some people haven’t said—that don’t think it has.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Ultimately, it’s unknowable, and so really again, what we’re focused on is, you know, looking at the data and giving ourselves a little more time now to look carefully at the data by being careful in our moves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s the question we’re asking ourselves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think, you know, years from now economists will be revising their estimates of r* as it existed on November 1, 2023.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can’t—we can’t really wait for that in making policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have to look—we have to have those models and look at them and think about them, and, ultimately, we’ve got to look at the effects that policy is having, accounting for the lags, which makes it difficult.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, if you look at the—look at the broad range of wages, they have—wage increases have really come down significantly over the course of the last 18 months to a level where they’re substantially closer to that level that would be consistent with 2 percent inflation over time, making standard assumptions about productivity over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s much closer than it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s true of the ECI, which is the one that’s—the one that we got this week.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s true of average hourly earnings and compensation per hour, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—and all of them are kind of saying that, which is great.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you have to look at a group of them because any one of them can be idiosyncratic from—in any given reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what you see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so what you saw with the ECI reading was, if you look back a couple—it comes out four times a year—if you look back a couple of quarters, you’ll see it was much higher, then it came down substantially in June.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then the September reading was more or less at the same level as the June reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, in a way, it’s just validating that decline, and it was very close to our expectations internally, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think we feel good about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Also I would say it isn’t—in my thinking, it’s not the case that, that wages have been the principal driver of inflation so far, although I think it’s all—I do think it’s fair to say that, as we go forward, as monetary policy becomes more important relative to the supply-side issues I’ve talked about in the unwinding of the pandemic effects, it may be that the labor market becomes more important over time, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, as I mentioned, I think for much of the last year and a half, the concern was not doing too, too—not doing enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It was not getting rates high enough in time to avoid having inflation expectations—higher inflation expectations become entrenched.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that was the concern.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we’ve reached, you know, now more than 18 months into this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can see by the fact that we have slowed down, although we’re still—we’re still—we’re still trying to gain confidence in what the appropriate stance is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you can see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think, and I think, that the risks are getting more balanced.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’ll just say that they’re getting more balanced.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The risk of doing too much versus the risk of doing too little are getting—are getting more—closer to balance, because policy is I think clearly restrictive at 5¼ to 5½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That range, if you take off a mainstream estimate of the expected inflation, take one year inflation, you’re going to see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re going to see a real policy rate that is well above mainstream estimates of a neutral policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now that’s arithmetic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It doesn’t really—the proof is really in how the economy reacts, but I would say that we’re in a place where those risks are getting closer to being in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Do we—is it sort of validating the path we saw over the summer, where inflation was clearly cooling and coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Now we’ve seen periods like that before, and they’ve just—there hasn’t been follow-through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The data have bounced back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s the first thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The second thing is, in the labor market, what we’ve seen is a very positive rebalancing of supply and demand, partly through just much more supply coming online.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And with labor demand still clearly remaining very strong—when you have the kind of job growth we’ve had over the last quarter, it’s still very strong demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—and you see wage increases coming down as we discussed but coming down in a kind of gradual way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think that’s—we want to see that, that whole set of processes continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t say there’s been a structural change in consumption.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would say it’s certainly been strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so a couple of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We may have underestimated the balance sheet strength of households and small businesses, and that may be part of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There may be—you know, we’ve been, like everyone else, trying to estimate the number—the amount of savings that households have from the pandemic when they couldn’t spend on services really at all, or in-person services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, there can still be more of that than we think, although at a certain point we have to—we’re going to be getting back to pre-pandemic levels of savings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We may not be there yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So things are—clearly, people are still spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The dynamic has been really strong job creation with now wages that are—that are higher than inflation, in the aggregate anyway, and that raises real disposable income, and that raises spending, which continues to drive more hiring.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so you’ve had a really—that whole—that whole dynamic has been, and also at the same time, the pandemic effects are wearing off, so that goods availability, automobile availability is better—or was better, I think it still is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, from a business standpoint, there are more people to hire.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it is more labor supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the whole thing has led to more growth, more spending, and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s been—you know, it’s been good, and the thing is, we’ve been achieving progress on inflation in the middle of this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, it’s been a dynamic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, I just think this—the existence of this second set of factors at this time, which is the unwinding of the pandemic effects, that’s what makes this cycle unique, I think, and, you know, we’re still learning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That took longer for that process to begin than we thought, and we’re still learning about how it plays out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s all we can do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t want to speculate too much, but I’ll just say so—you know, really the question there is, does the war spread more widely and does it start to do things like affect oil prices in particular, since this is the Middle East we’re talking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The price of oil has really not reacted very much so far to this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As the—you know, as the Fed—as the Federal Open Market Committee, our job is really to talk about [and] to understand the economy and economic effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it isn’t clear, at this point, that the conflict in the Middle East is going to—is on track to have significant economic effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That doesn’t mean it isn’t incredibly important and something for people to, you know, to take really important notice of, but it may or may not turn out to be something that matters for the Federal Open Market Committee as an economic body.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But—so what the Financial Stability Report does is it “calls out” risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what it’s doing—[it] is calling out a risk of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the war in Ukraine, the same.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The war in Ukraine did have, immediately, very significant macroeconomic implications because of the connection to commodities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thanks very much.
